title: Quiz: Formula Notation, Model Matrix, and Categorical Predictors

questions.text: In the formula y ~ x1 + x2, what does the '+' operator do?
options: It adds the values of x1 and x2 together before using them as a predictor
It specifies that x1 and x2 are both included as separate additive predictors in the model
It creates an interaction term between x1 and x2
It squares x1 and adds x2
questions.explanation: In R formula notation, '+' means 'include this predictor in the model additively.' The model y ~ x1 + x2 means y = β₀ + β₁x1 + β₂x2 + ε — two separate predictors with separate coefficients. To create an interaction, use '*' or ':'.

questions.text: For a factor with 5 levels, R creates 5 dummy variable columns in the design matrix.
questions.explanation: R creates k − 1 = 4 dummy columns for a factor with k = 5 levels. The reference level (first by default) is represented by all four dummies being 0. Including all k dummies would create perfect multicollinearity (the dummy columns sum to the intercept column), making X'X singular.

questions.text: In lm(log(price) ~ log(carat) + cut), the coefficient for cutIdeal is 0.40. What does this mean?
options: Ideal diamonds cost $0.40 more than Fair diamonds
Ideal diamonds cost 40% more than Fair diamonds regardless of carat
Holding carat constant, Ideal-cut diamonds have a log(price) that is 0.40 units higher than Fair-cut, i.e., exp(0.40) ≈ 1.49 times the price of Fair
The model R² improves by 0.40 when cut is added
questions.explanation: In a log-response model, a coefficient of 0.40 means log(price) is 0.40 units higher for Ideal vs Fair (holding carat constant). Back-transforming: exp(0.40) ≈ 1.49, so Ideal diamonds cost about 49% more than Fair diamonds of the same carat weight.

questions.text: You change the reference level of 'cut' from 'Fair' to 'Ideal' using relevel(). How does this affect R²?
options: R² increases because Ideal is a better reference level
R² decreases because fewer dummy variables are in the model
R² is unchanged — re-parameterisation does not affect model fit
R² changes only if the sample size is small
questions.explanation: Changing the reference level is a pure re-parameterisation. The fitted values ŷᵢ are identical regardless of which level is the reference, so RSS, TSS, and therefore R² are unchanged. Only the interpretation of individual coefficients changes.

questions.text: Without controlling for carat, Ideal-cut diamonds appear cheaper than Fair-cut. But after adding log(carat) to the model, Ideal has a positive coefficient. What statistical phenomenon explains this?
options: Confounding — carat is correlated with both cut and price, distorting the raw cut-price relationship
Selection bias in how diamonds were sampled
questions.explanation: Confounding (related to Simpson's Paradox): cut and carat are correlated (lower-quality cuts are applied to larger, heavier rough stones). In the raw data, cut is 'confounded' by carat — the apparent cheapness of Ideal is really the smallness of Ideal diamonds. Once we control for carat in the regression, the genuine quality premium of Ideal cut is revealed.

questions.text: In R, the formula y ~ . (dot) includes all columns in the data frame as predictors.
questions.explanation: The dot shorthand y ~ . means 'use all other columns in the data frame as predictors.' It is convenient for exploratory modelling but can inadvertently include ID columns, date columns, or the response variable itself if the data frame is not carefully prepared.
